history.q: Whose nearly intact tomb did Howard Carter discover in the Valley of the Kings in 1922?
history.fact: Tomb KV62 held more than 5,000 objects, including the famous gold funerary mask.

history.q: Which Macedonian conqueror founded the city of Alexandria in 331 BCE?
history.fact: Alexandria's Pharos lighthouse was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and its Great Library became a legendary centre of learning.

history.q: Who was the last active ruler of Egypt's Ptolemaic Kingdom before it became a Roman province in 30 BCE?
history.fact: According to Plutarch, Cleopatra spoke many languages and was the first of her Greek-Macedonian dynasty to learn Egyptian.

history.q: The Rosetta Stone was found in 1799 during which military campaign?
history.fact: Its 196 BCE decree appears in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, which helped Jean-François Champollion decipher hieroglyphs in 1822.

history.q: Which pharaoh fought the Hittites at the Battle of Kadesh around 1274 BCE?
history.fact: A later peace treaty between Ramesses II and the Hittites (c. 1259 BCE) is one of the earliest known; a replica is displayed at the UN in New York.

history.q: Which king is traditionally credited with unifying Upper and Lower Egypt around 3100 BCE?
history.fact: The Narmer Palette shows him wearing the white crown of Upper Egypt on one side and the red crown of Lower Egypt on the other.

history.q: Which female pharaoh of the 18th Dynasty built a terraced mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari?
history.fact: She sent a celebrated trading expedition to the Land of Punt, shown in her temple's reliefs, which brought back incense trees.

history.q: In which year did the Suez Canal open to shipping?
history.fact: The canal has no locks: the Mediterranean and Red Sea are close enough in level that ships sail straight through.

history.q: Pharaoh Akhenaten built a new capital devoted to the sun disc Aten. What was it called?
history.fact: Today called Amarna, the site yielded the 'Amarna letters', diplomatic tablets written in Akkadian cuneiform.

history.q: Which dynasty founded the city of Cairo in 969 CE?
history.fact: The Fatimids also founded Al-Azhar Mosque in 970-972; its university is one of the oldest continuously operating in the world.

history.q: Which Roman general was Cleopatra's ally and partner when their fleet was defeated at Actium in 31 BCE?
history.fact: After Actium, Octavian pursued the pair to Alexandria, where both died in 30 BCE and Egypt became Roman.

history.q: Which European power occupied Egypt in 1882?
history.fact: British troops landed in 1882 and stayed in parts of Egypt for 74 years, until the last soldiers left the Suez Canal zone in 1956.

history.q: Which sultan, founder of the Ayyubid dynasty, ruled Egypt and captured Jerusalem in 1187?
history.fact: Saladin began building the Cairo Citadel in 1176; it remained the seat of Egypt's rulers for nearly 700 years.

history.q: Egypt's 2011 revolution centred on mass protests in which Cairo square?
history.fact: "Tahrir" means "liberation" in Arabic; the square was originally named after the 19th-century ruler Khedive Ismail.

history.q: What was the main purpose of the pyramids of ancient Egypt?
history.fact: Egypt has more than 100 known pyramids, built over about a thousand years as burial monuments for kings and queens.

history.q: Which empire conquered Egypt from the Mamluks in 1517?
history.fact: Sultan Selim I took Cairo in 1517, and Egypt stayed formally part of the Ottoman Empire until 1914.

history.q: Which Arab general led the Muslim conquest of Egypt in the 640s?
history.fact: Amr founded the garrison city of Fustat, whose mosque, the Mosque of Amr ibn al-As, was the first built in Egypt.

history.q: At which 1260 battle did Egypt's Mamluks halt the advance of the Mongols?
history.fact: Ain Jalut, in Palestine, was one of the first major battles the Mongols lost, and it made the Mamluks the leading power of the region.

history.q: Which general of Alexander the Great founded the dynasty that ruled Egypt until Cleopatra?
history.fact: Ptolemy I is said to have hijacked Alexander's body on its way to Macedonia and buried it in Egypt to boost his own legitimacy.

history.q: Which 1942 battle in Egypt's Western Desert was a turning point of the North African campaign?
history.fact: Churchill later said, "Before Alamein we never had a victory. After Alamein we never had a defeat."

history.q: Which foreign rulers controlled northern Egypt before being driven out by Ahmose I around 1550 BCE?
history.fact: The Hyksos are credited with bringing the horse-drawn chariot into wide use in Egypt.

history.q: Rulers of Egypt's 25th Dynasty came from which kingdom to the south?
history.fact: Kushite kings from what is now Sudan ruled Egypt for about a century and built their own pyramids at Nuri and Meroe.

history.q: Which Persian king conquered Egypt in 525 BCE?
history.fact: Cambyses won at the Battle of Pelusium, and Egypt became a province, or satrapy, of the Achaemenid Persian Empire.

history.q: Which army officer led the nationalist revolt defeated by the British at Tel el-Kebir in 1882?
history.fact: After his defeat Urabi was exiled to Ceylon (Sri Lanka), where he lived for almost 20 years before returning to Egypt.

history.q: Which woman ruled Egypt as sultana in 1250, between the Ayyubid and Mamluk eras?
history.fact: Shajar al-Durr had coins struck in her own name, a rare honour for a woman ruler in the medieval Islamic world.

technology.q: What writing material did ancient Egyptians make from a reed that grew along the Nile?
technology.fact: The English word 'paper' comes from 'papyrus'. Sheets were made by laying strips of the plant's pith crosswise and pressing them together.

technology.q: Who is credited as the architect of the Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara?
technology.fact: Built around the 27th century BCE, it is one of the oldest large stone buildings; Imhotep was later revered as a god of medicine.

technology.q: How many days were in the ancient Egyptian civil calendar year?
technology.fact: It had 12 months of 30 days plus 5 extra days at year's end, celebrated as the birthdays of gods including Osiris and Isis.

technology.q: Which Egyptian-born scientist won the 1999 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for femtochemistry?
technology.fact: Femtochemistry uses ultrafast laser flashes to watch atoms move during chemical reactions, on timescales of a millionth of a billionth of a second.

technology.q: Which major dam on the Nile, completed in 1970, created Lake Nasser?
technology.fact: Lake Nasser stretches for hundreds of kilometres and crosses into Sudan, where its southern part is called Lake Nubia.

technology.q: Working in Alexandria around 240 BCE, which scholar estimated Earth's circumference by comparing shadows?
technology.fact: He compared the Sun's angle at Syene (modern Aswan) and at Alexandria; his estimate was remarkably close to the true value.

technology.q: What structure did ancient Egyptians use to measure the Nile's flood level?
technology.fact: Flood readings helped officials predict harvests and set taxes. The Nilometer on Cairo's Roda Island dates to 861 CE.

technology.q: During mummification, internal organs were stored in which kind of container?
technology.fact: There were usually four jars, their lids often shaped as the four Sons of Horus, guarding the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines.

technology.q: Which scribe copied the Rhind Mathematical Papyrus around 1550 BCE?
technology.fact: Its 80-plus problems cover fractions, areas and volumes. The papyrus is now held in the British Museum.

technology.q: The Edwin Smith Papyrus is one of the oldest known texts on which subject?
technology.fact: It describes 48 injury cases, each with an examination, diagnosis and treatment, in a remarkably practical style.

technology.q: Which Wonder of the Ancient World stood on the island of Pharos at Alexandria?
technology.fact: The lighthouse was so famous that "pharos" became the word for lighthouse in Greek, French (phare) and Italian (faro).

technology.q: What is the name of the picture-based writing system of ancient Egypt?
technology.fact: The word hieroglyph comes from Greek for "sacred carvings"; the system used several hundred signs.

technology.q: Which French diplomat led the company that built the Suez Canal?
technology.fact: De Lesseps later tried to build a canal in Panama too, but the French effort failed amid disease and financial scandal.

technology.q: Which Greek mathematician, known as the "father of geometry", worked in Alexandria around 300 BCE?
technology.fact: Euclid's Elements was used as a geometry textbook for over 2,000 years.

technology.q: What ancient Egyptian unit of length was based on the forearm?
technology.fact: The royal cubit was about 52 cm long and was divided into seven palms of four fingers each.

technology.q: Which astronomer working in Alexandria wrote the Almagest, which placed Earth at the centre of the universe?
technology.fact: The Almagest's Earth-centred model remained the standard astronomy text in Europe and the Islamic world for about 1,400 years.

technology.q: Which mathematician and philosopher taught in Alexandria until her death in 415 CE?
technology.fact: Hypatia's father Theon was also a mathematician, and she is believed to have helped edit his work on Ptolemy's astronomy.

technology.q: What is the name of the pivoting pole-and-bucket device used in Egypt since ancient times to lift water?
technology.fact: Tomb paintings show the shaduf over 3,000 years ago, and farmers along the Nile still used it in the 20th century.

technology.q: The ancient Egyptian year was linked to the dawn rising of which star, just before the Nile flood?
technology.fact: Egyptians called Sirius Sopdet; its reappearance before sunrise each summer heralded the life-giving inundation.

technology.q: Which inventor in Roman-era Alexandria described the aeolipile, a spinning steam-powered sphere?
technology.fact: Hero also described a coin-operated holy water dispenser, often called the world's first vending machine.

technology.q: Egyptian blue, made by heating silica, lime, copper and an alkali, is often called the earliest known synthetic what?
technology.fact: Egyptian blue glows in infrared light, which lets scientists detect faint traces of it on ancient objects.

technology.q: Which Alexandrian engineer of the 3rd century BCE is credited with inventing the force pump and an improved water clock?
technology.fact: Ctesibius is also credited with the hydraulis, a water-powered pipe organ that was an ancestor of the church organ.

technology.q: Which scholar, working in Fatimid Cairo in the 11th century, wrote the influential Book of Optics?
technology.fact: Ibn al-Haytham argued that we see because light enters the eye, overturning the old idea that eyes send out rays.

technology.q: The Moscow Mathematical Papyrus contains a famous calculation of the volume of which shape?
technology.fact: The papyrus is about 3,800 years old, yet its method for a truncated pyramid, or frustum, matches the modern formula.

technology.q: Egyptian-born Sir Magdi Yacoub is a world-renowned pioneer in which field?
technology.fact: Yacoub led a pioneering heart transplant programme at Harefield Hospital in Britain and later founded a heart centre in Aswan.

art.q: A famous painted limestone bust in Berlin's Neues Museum depicts which queen?
art.fact: Made around 1345 BCE, it was found in 1912 in the Amarna workshop of the sculptor Thutmose.

art.q: Which Egyptian writer won the 1988 Nobel Prize in Literature?
art.fact: He was the first Arabic-language writer to win; his Cairo Trilogy follows one family across three generations.

art.q: The Great Sphinx of Giza has a human head on the body of which animal?
art.fact: It was carved directly from the limestone bedrock of the Giza plateau and is about 73 m long.

art.q: Which collection of spells, written on papyrus and placed in tombs, was meant to guide the dead through the afterlife?
art.fact: Its Egyptian title means roughly 'Book of Coming Forth by Day'. One famous scene shows the heart weighed against the feather of Ma'at.

art.q: Which Egyptian singer was nicknamed 'Kawkab al-Sharq' (Star of the East)?
art.fact: Her monthly live radio concerts drew huge audiences across the Arab world, and a single song could stretch beyond an hour.

art.q: In the 1960s, which organization led the international campaign to relocate the Abu Simbel temples away from rising waters?
art.fact: The temples of Ramesses II were cut into huge blocks and reassembled about 65 m higher, a rescue that inspired the World Heritage system.

art.q: Which Egyptian director made the classic film 'Cairo Station' (1958)?
art.fact: Chahine also starred in the film as a newspaper seller, and received a lifetime achievement prize at Cannes in 1997.

art.q: Egyptian actor Omar Sharif earned an Oscar nomination for which 1962 film?
art.fact: Sharif was also a world-class contract bridge player who wrote newspaper columns about the game.

art.q: Lifelike portraits painted on wooden panels and placed over mummies in Roman-era Egypt are named after which region?
art.fact: Many were painted in encaustic, pigment mixed with hot wax, and they are among the most realistic portraits surviving from antiquity.

art.q: Which Cairo mosque, completed in 879 CE, is known for a minaret with an external spiral staircase?
art.fact: Its founder, Ahmad ibn Tulun, grew up in Samarra, Iraq, and the spiral minaret echoes the famous Great Mosque of Samarra.

art.q: Which Verdi opera, set in ancient Egypt, premiered in Cairo in 1871?
art.fact: Aida was commissioned by Khedive Ismail; its plot was sketched by the French Egyptologist Auguste Mariette.

art.q: In ancient Egyptian painting, a person's head is usually shown from which angle?
art.fact: Artists combined the most recognizable views: the head in profile, but the eye and shoulders drawn as if seen from the front.

art.q: Which vast temple complex at Luxor, dedicated chiefly to Amun, is famous for its Great Hypostyle Hall?
art.fact: The Great Hypostyle Hall at Karnak has 134 massive columns, some about 21 m tall.

art.q: In hieroglyphic inscriptions, what does an oval ring called a cartouche enclose?
art.fact: The cartouches on the Rosetta Stone, holding the name Ptolemy, were a key to cracking hieroglyphs.

art.q: What kind of ancient Egyptian monument stands in the centre of Paris's Place de la Concorde?
art.fact: The 3,000-year-old Luxor Obelisk was a gift from Egypt's ruler and was raised in Paris in 1836.

art.q: Whose tomb in the Valley of the Queens is celebrated as one of the most beautifully painted in Egypt?
art.fact: Nefertari was the chief wife of Ramesses II, who also dedicated the smaller temple at Abu Simbel to her.

art.q: What is the Arabic name for the solo dance style known in the West as belly dance?
art.fact: Raqs sharqi means "oriental dance"; Egyptian films of the 1930s-50s made its star dancers famous across the Arab world.

art.q: Which Egyptian poet was hailed as the "Prince of Poets" in 1927?
art.fact: Shawqi also wrote verse dramas, including one on Cleopatra, which helped bring theatre into modern Arabic poetry.

art.q: Which Egyptian singer and actor was nicknamed "the Dark Nightingale"?
art.fact: Abdel Halim's 1977 funeral in Cairo drew huge crowds, and his romantic songs remain staples of Arabic radio.

art.q: Which Egyptian novelist wrote "The Yacoubian Building" (2002)?
art.fact: The novel follows the residents of a real downtown Cairo apartment block and became one of the best-selling Arabic novels.

art.q: The Colossi of Memnon near Luxor depict which pharaoh?
art.fact: After an earthquake cracked one statue, it "sang" at dawn, drawing Roman tourists who carved graffiti on its legs.

art.q: Which sculptor created "Egypt's Awakening", the granite monument near Cairo University?
art.fact: The statue shows a peasant woman lifting her veil beside a rising sphinx, a symbol of the nation after 1919.

art.q: Which poet from Alexandria wrote "Ithaka" and "Waiting for the Barbarians"?
art.fact: Cavafy wrote in Greek and spent most of his life in Alexandria, working as a clerk for decades.

art.q: Which composer wrote the music for Umm Kulthum's famous 1964 song "Enta Omri"?
art.fact: Enta Omri was nicknamed "the meeting of the giants" because it united Egypt's greatest singer and greatest composer.

art.q: Who directed the 1969 Egyptian film "The Night of Counting the Years" (Al-Mummia)?
art.fact: The film is about the 1881 discovery of a royal mummy cache and is often voted among the best Arab films ever made.

politics.q: Which Egyptian president nationalized the Suez Canal in 1956?
politics.fact: He announced the nationalization in a speech in Alexandria on 26 July 1956, sparking the Suez Crisis.

politics.q: Which Egyptian president signed the Camp David Accords with Israel in 1978?
politics.fact: Sadat shared the 1978 Nobel Peace Prize with Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin.

politics.q: Who served as Egypt's president from 1981 to 2011?
politics.fact: He stepped down in February 2011 after 18 days of mass protests centred on Cairo's Tahrir Square.

politics.q: Which regional organization was founded in Cairo in 1945 and is headquartered there?
politics.fact: Its headquarters moved to Tunis from 1979 to 1990 before returning to Cairo.

politics.q: Who became Egypt's first president when the republic was declared in 1953?
politics.fact: A leading figure of the 1952 revolution, he was sidelined by Nasser in 1954 and spent years under house arrest.

politics.q: Which Egyptian diplomat served as UN Secretary-General from 1992 to 1996?
politics.fact: He was the first UN Secretary-General from Africa and the Arab world.

politics.q: Which Egyptian diplomat led the International Atomic Energy Agency and shared the 2005 Nobel Peace Prize with it?
politics.fact: He headed the IAEA, the UN's nuclear watchdog based in Vienna, from 1997 to 2009.

politics.q: Which nationalist leader inspired Egypt's 1919 revolution against British rule and later became prime minister?
politics.fact: His exile by the British in 1919 sparked nationwide protests; he led the Wafd Party and became prime minister in 1924.

politics.q: Which ruler took the title King of Egypt when Britain recognized Egyptian independence in 1922?
politics.fact: His son Farouk succeeded him in 1936 and abdicated after the 1952 revolution.

politics.q: Which Ottoman-appointed governor, who took power in 1805, is often called the founder of modern Egypt?
politics.fact: His dynasty ruled Egypt until 1952, and his domed mosque crowns the skyline of Cairo's Citadel.

politics.q: Which king of Egypt was forced to abdicate after the 1952 revolution?
politics.fact: Farouk sailed into exile from Alexandria on the royal yacht; his infant son Fuad II was nominally king for under a year.

politics.q: What was the group of army officers that overthrew Egypt's monarchy in 1952 called?
politics.fact: The coup of 23 July 1952 is still marked as Revolution Day, a national holiday in Egypt.

politics.q: In the October War of 1973, Egypt and Syria fought against which country?
politics.fact: Egyptian forces crossed the Suez Canal on 6 October 1973; the date gives its name to a Cairo bridge and a city near Giza.

politics.q: Who won Egypt's 2012 presidential election, the first held after the 2011 revolution?
politics.fact: The 2012 vote went to a run-off, which Morsi won with about 52% against Ahmed Shafik.

politics.q: During the 1956 Suez Crisis, Egypt was invaded by Israel, Britain and which other country?
politics.fact: Pressure from the US and USSR forced a withdrawal, and the first armed UN peacekeeping force was sent in.

politics.q: Which political union did Egypt form with Syria from 1958 to 1961?
politics.fact: Egypt kept the name United Arab Republic for a decade after Syria left, until 1971.

politics.q: From 1899 to 1956, Sudan was jointly governed by Britain and Egypt under what arrangement?
politics.fact: Under the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium both flags flew over Khartoum, though Britain held most real power.

politics.q: Which movement was founded in Ismailia in 1928 by Hassan al-Banna?
politics.fact: Ismailia, the Suez Canal town where al-Banna taught school, was founded by the Suez Canal Company in the 1860s.

politics.q: In which 1967 war did Egypt lose control of the Sinai Peninsula?
politics.fact: Most of Sinai was returned by 1982 under the 1979 peace treaty; the small resort of Taba followed in 1989 after arbitration.

politics.q: Which former Egyptian foreign minister served as Secretary-General of the Arab League from 2001 to 2011?
politics.fact: Amr Moussa later chaired the committee that drafted Egypt's 2014 constitution.

politics.q: Which British consul-general effectively ran Egypt's government from 1883 to 1907?
politics.fact: Evelyn Baring, Lord Cromer, came from the Barings banking family and was sent to sort out Egypt's debts.

politics.q: In which year did Britain declare Egypt a protectorate, formally ending Ottoman sovereignty?
politics.fact: Britain made the move at the outbreak of the First World War, as the Ottoman Empire joined Germany's side.

politics.q: Which head of the Supreme Constitutional Court served as Egypt's interim president from July 2013 to June 2014?
politics.fact: A judge by career, Mansour did not run for president himself and returned to the judiciary after his interim term.

politics.q: What was the name of the nationalist party that grew out of Saad Zaghloul's 1918 delegation to the British?
politics.fact: Wafd simply means "delegation" in Arabic, after the group that asked to plead Egypt's case for independence.

politics.q: Which khedive sold Egypt's shares in the Suez Canal Company to Britain in 1875?
politics.fact: Ismail dreamed of making Egypt "part of Europe" and rebuilt central Cairo in Parisian style, but sank into huge debts.

current-affairs.q: Which container ship blocked the Suez Canal for six days in March 2021?
current-affairs.fact: The 400 m-long ship was freed with help from dredgers, tugs and a high spring tide, while hundreds of vessels queued at each end.

current-affairs.q: Which Egyptian city hosted the COP27 UN climate conference in November 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Delegates agreed to create a 'loss and damage' fund to help vulnerable countries cope with climate impacts.

current-affairs.q: Who won Egypt's presidential election held in December 2023?
current-affairs.fact: It was his third term; 2019 constitutional amendments had extended presidential terms from four years to six.

current-affairs.q: Egyptian forward Mohamed Salah helped which club win the 2024-25 Premier League title?
current-affairs.fact: Salah scored 29 league goals that season, winning the Golden Boot and the Premier League Player of the Season award.

current-affairs.q: In April 2021's 'Pharaohs' Golden Parade', 22 royal mummies were moved to which museum?
current-affairs.fact: The 18 kings and 4 queens, including Ramesses II and Hatshepsut, travelled through Cairo in specially built, shock-absorbing vehicles.

current-affairs.q: In November 2021, Egypt reopened an ancient processional avenue lined with sphinxes linking two temples in which city?
current-affairs.fact: The roughly 2.7 km avenue connects the Karnak and Luxor temples and once hosted processions of the ancient Opet Festival.

current-affairs.q: Egypt became a full member of which group of nations on 1 January 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Egypt joined alongside Ethiopia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates in the group's first expansion since South Africa's entry.

current-affairs.q: In October 2024, the World Health Organization certified Egypt free of which disease?
current-affairs.fact: The WHO noted malaria had been present in Egypt since ancient times; genetic traces of the parasite were found in Tutankhamun's mummy.

current-affairs.q: In 2023, Egypt became the first country to reach WHO 'gold tier' status on the path to eliminating which disease?
current-affairs.fact: Its '100 Million Healthy Lives' campaign, launched in 2018, screened tens of millions of people and offered free treatment.

current-affairs.q: In March 2023, scientists announced a hidden corridor about 9 m long behind the north face of which pyramid?
current-affairs.fact: The ScanPyramids project detected it using muons, particles created by cosmic rays, then confirmed it with an endoscope camera.

current-affairs.q: Which giant museum beside the Giza plateau held its official grand opening in November 2025?
current-affairs.fact: The museum displays Tutankhamun's complete treasure together for the first time, and a colossal Ramesses II greets visitors.

current-affairs.q: In 2024, Suez Canal revenues fell sharply as many ships avoided attacks on shipping in which sea?
current-affairs.fact: Many container lines rerouted around Africa's Cape of Good Hope, a detour adding roughly 10 days to Asia-Europe trips.

current-affairs.q: Which Cairo football club won the CAF Champions League in both 2023 and 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Al Ahly's 2024 victory was its 12th African title, a record for the competition.

current-affairs.q: Which country began filling the reservoir of the Grand Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile in 2020?
current-affairs.fact: The Blue Nile supplies most of the water that reaches Egypt, which is why the dam has been a long-running regional issue.

current-affairs.q: Which crossing on Egypt's border with the Gaza Strip became a focus of international aid efforts from October 2023?
current-affairs.fact: Rafah was Gaza's only crossing that did not lead into Israel, which made it a vital gateway for people and supplies.

current-affairs.q: Which skyscraper in Egypt's New Administrative Capital, about 394 m tall, became Africa's tallest building in the early 2020s?
current-affairs.fact: The New Administrative Capital is being built in the desert about 45 km east of Cairo as a new seat of government.

current-affairs.q: Egypt hosted the 2019 Africa Cup of Nations; which country won it?
current-affairs.fact: Algeria beat Senegal 1-0 in the Cairo final for its second continental title, 29 years after its first.

current-affairs.q: In which sport did Egypt's Ahmed Elgendy win Olympic gold at Paris 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Elgendy had already won silver at the Tokyo Games; modern pentathlon combines fencing, swimming, riding, running and shooting.

current-affairs.q: In 2020, Egypt unveiled more than 100 sealed wooden coffins, about 2,500 years old, found at which necropolis?
current-affairs.fact: Some of the painted coffins were opened in front of the press, revealing well-preserved mummies inside.

current-affairs.q: In April 2021, which Egyptologist announced the discovery of a 3,000-year-old "lost golden city" near Luxor?
current-affairs.fact: The city dates to the reign of Amenhotep III and was nicknamed "the Rise of Aten".

current-affairs.q: In February 2024, investors from which country agreed a $35 billion deal to develop Egypt's Ras El-Hekma peninsula?
current-affairs.fact: Ras El-Hekma is a stretch of Mediterranean coast west of Alexandria, planned as a new resort and business city.

current-affairs.q: At which site did Egypt begin building its first nuclear power plant in 2022?
current-affairs.fact: The plant, built with Russia's Rosatom on the Mediterranean coast, is designed to have four large reactors.

current-affairs.q: At the Tokyo Olympics held in 2021, Feryal Abdelaziz became the first Egyptian woman to win Olympic gold, in which sport?
current-affairs.fact: Karate was making its Olympic debut in Tokyo, so Abdelaziz was among the sport's very first Olympic champions.

current-affairs.q: Which Egyptian club won its first CAF Champions League title in 2025?
current-affairs.fact: The club, which took its current name only in 2018, beat South Africa's Mamelodi Sundowns in the final.

current-affairs.q: The Benban solar park, one of the world's largest when completed in 2019, lies near which Egyptian city?
current-affairs.fact: Benban spreads millions of solar panels over roughly 37 square km of desert, among the sunniest land on Earth.

society.q: In February 2020, Egypt's population officially passed which milestone?
society.fact: The statistics agency CAPMAS marked the moment on a live population counter in Cairo; Egypt is the most populous Arab country.

society.q: After Egypt let its currency float in March 2024, roughly how many Egyptian pounds bought one US dollar?
society.fact: The pound fell from about 31 to the dollar overnight, having already lost half its value in a series of devaluations since early 2022.

society.q: Egypt's annual urban inflation rate peaked in September 2023 at roughly what level?
society.fact: It was a record for Egypt, driven by a weaker pound and import costs; food inflation was even higher at over 70%.

society.q: From 2023, Egypt's government ministries began moving out of Cairo to which newly built city?
society.fact: Built in the desert about 45 km east of Cairo since 2015, it is intended to relieve pressure on the capital, home to over 20 million people.

society.q: In the summers of 2023 and 2024, Egypt imposed scheduled daily cuts to what because of a natural gas shortage?
society.fact: Rolling blackouts of up to three hours a day hit homes and businesses in heatwaves; they ended in July 2024 after emergency fuel imports.

society.q: In June 2024, Egypt raised the price of subsidised bread for the first time in roughly how many years?
society.fact: The price of a subsidised loaf rose from 5 to 20 piastres, still a fraction of its cost; around 70 million Egyptians rely on the scheme.

society.q: From 2023, Egypt took in large numbers of people fleeing a war in which neighbouring country?
society.fact: By 2024 the UN estimated over a million people had crossed from Sudan, adding to pressure on housing and services in Cairo and Aswan.

society.q: Egypt recorded a record number of tourist arrivals in 2024, roughly how many?
society.fact: About 15.7 million visitors came, beating the 2023 record; tourism is a key source of foreign currency and employs millions of Egyptians.

society.q: What is the name of Egypt's long-term national development strategy, launched in 2016?
society.fact: It sets targets across the economy, education and health, and is aligned with the UN Sustainable Development Goals.

society.q: In March 2024, the IMF increased its loan programme for Egypt to a total of what?
society.fact: The original $3 billion deal of December 2022 was expanded after Egypt devalued the pound and raised interest rates by six percentage points.

society.q: In 2024, Egypt raised the minimum monthly wage for public sector workers to what amount?
society.fact: It was raised from EGP 4,000 as part of a package to cushion inflation, and lifted again to EGP 7,000 in 2025.

society.q: Egypt's official poverty rate in 2019/20 was roughly what share of the population?
society.fact: CAPMAS put it at 29.7%, the first fall in two decades, down from 32.5% in 2017/18.

society.q: Egypt's official unemployment rate in 2023 was roughly what?
society.fact: CAPMAS put it at 7.1% in the third quarter of 2023; the rate for women (about 17%) is far higher than for men, and many jobs are informal.

society.q: Roughly how many Egyptians were covered by state food ration cards in the early 2020s?
society.fact: The 'tamween' cards give monthly allowances for staples such as cooking oil, sugar and rice; the government has moved to trim the rolls.

society.q: Under a 2019 law, Egypt's retirement age is to rise gradually from 60 to what?
society.fact: Under Law 148 of 2019 the increase begins in July 2032, rising one year every two years to reach 65 by 2040, to keep the pension system solvent.

society.q: In 2024, Egypt went back to being a net importer of which fuel, having exported it since 2019?
society.fact: Output from the giant Zohr field declined faster than expected, forcing Egypt to buy liquefied natural gas cargoes during summer power shortages.

society.q: What was the name of the family-planning campaign Egypt launched in 2018 to slow population growth?
society.fact: 'Etnein Kefaya' targeted rural families; Egypt's fertility rate has since fallen from about 3.5 to under 2.5 children per woman.

society.q: Egypt's economy grew by roughly what in fiscal year 2019/20, when most economies shrank?
society.fact: Egypt was one of the few emerging economies to avoid recession in 2020, helped by state construction projects and remittances.

society.q: In 2022, Egypt signed a deal with which company to build a roughly 2,000 km high-speed rail network?
society.fact: The €8.1 billion contract is Siemens Mobility's largest ever order; the first line links the Red Sea coast with Alexandria via the new capital.

society.q: 'Hayah Karima' (Decent Life), launched in 2019, is an Egyptian initiative to do what?
society.fact: Expanded in 2021 to more than 4,000 villages, it provides water, sewage, housing and clinics and is described as the largest development project in Egypt's history.

society.q: 'Takaful and Karama', expanded through the 2020s, is Egypt's programme providing what?
society.fact: Takaful pays mothers conditional on children's school attendance and health checks; Karama supports the elderly and disabled.

society.q: In 2019, Egypt began rolling out its universal health insurance system, starting in which governorate?
society.fact: The scheme is being phased in governorate by governorate over about 15 years, replacing a patchwork of older insurance funds.

society.q: What is the standard rate of value-added tax in Egypt, set in 2017?
society.fact: VAT replaced the old sales tax in 2016 at 13%, rising to 14% in 2017 as part of a reform programme agreed with the IMF.

society.q: Around 2023, roughly what share of Egyptian women of working age were in the labour force?
society.fact: It is among the lowest rates in the world, compared with about 70% for Egyptian men, despite women making up over half of university students.

society.q: The Egyptian-Japanese Schools, opened from 2018, teach a model of all-round education known by which Japanese word?
society.fact: Tokkatsu uses classroom cleaning, group activities and daily reflection to build character; dozens of such schools now operate across Egypt.

general.q: Which river flows north through Egypt to the Mediterranean Sea?
general.fact: Most Egyptians live in the narrow Nile Valley and Delta, a green ribbon covering only a small fraction of the country's land.

general.q: What is the currency of Egypt?
general.fact: The pound is divided into 100 piastres, and Egyptians often call it the 'geneih'.

general.q: Egypt's Sinai Peninsula forms a land bridge between Africa and which continent?
general.fact: At Sinai's southern tip, Ras Mohammed National Park protects some of the Red Sea's most spectacular coral reefs.

general.q: What is the nickname of Egypt's national football team?
general.fact: Egypt has won the Africa Cup of Nations a record seven times, including three in a row from 2006 to 2010.

general.q: Which popular Egyptian street dish combines rice, lentils, pasta and chickpeas topped with tomato sauce and crispy onions?
general.fact: Ta'ameya, Egypt's version of falafel, is traditionally made with fava beans rather than chickpeas.

general.q: Which language, descended from ancient Egyptian, is still used in the liturgy of Egypt's Coptic Church?
general.fact: Coptic is written in an alphabet based on Greek, plus several extra letters borrowed from Demotic Egyptian script.

general.q: What is Egypt's highest mountain?
general.fact: Rising about 2,629 m in southern Sinai, it stands near St Catherine's Monastery, one of the oldest working Christian monasteries.

general.q: The ancient city of Thebes lies at the site of which modern Egyptian city?
general.fact: Across the Nile on Luxor's West Bank lies the Valley of the Kings, burial ground of New Kingdom pharaohs.

general.q: Which depression in Egypt's Western Desert sinks to about 133 m below sea level?
general.fact: It is one of the lowest points in Africa, and its salt marshes were nearly impassable to armies during World War II.

general.q: Alexander the Great visited a famous oracle at Siwa Oasis dedicated to which god?
general.fact: Many of Siwa's people speak Siwi, a Berber (Amazigh) language, reflecting the oasis's long ties to North Africa's west.

general.q: What is the capital city of Egypt?
general.fact: Greater Cairo is home to over 20 million people, making it one of the largest urban areas in Africa and the Middle East.

general.q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World is the only one still standing?
general.fact: The Great Pyramid was originally covered in polished white limestone casing stones that would have gleamed in the sun.

general.q: Which jackal-headed Egyptian god was associated with mummification and the dead?
general.fact: Jackals prowled desert cemeteries, so Egyptians may have made a jackal god the protector of the dead.

general.q: What is the official language of Egypt?
general.fact: Egyptian Arabic is widely understood across the Arab world, thanks largely to Egypt's films and TV series.

general.q: Which desert covers most of Egypt?
general.fact: About 95% of Egyptians live on roughly 5% of the land, mostly along the Nile and in its delta.

general.q: Which Cairo mosque, founded in 970, is home to one of the world's oldest continuously operating universities?
general.fact: Al-Azhar was founded by the Fatimids and has drawn students from across the Muslim world for over a thousand years.

general.q: Which slow-cooked fava bean dish is a classic Egyptian breakfast?
general.fact: Ful has been simmered overnight in big copper pots for centuries, and street carts sell it across Cairo each morning.

general.q: Which Mediterranean port is Egypt's second-largest city?
general.fact: The modern Bibliotheca Alexandrina, opened in 2002, honours the city's famous ancient library.

general.q: Which city lies at the northern, Mediterranean end of the Suez Canal?
general.fact: Port Said was founded in 1859 when canal work began and is named after Said Pasha, the ruler who granted the concession.

general.q: Egyptian players have dominated the world rankings since the 2010s in which racket sport?
general.fact: Egypt has often held the top spots in both the men's and women's world squash rankings at the same time.

general.q: Which Egyptian spring festival, dating back to pharaonic times, is traditionally celebrated with salted fish and coloured eggs?
general.fact: Sham el-Nessim, meaning "smelling the breeze", falls on the Monday after Coptic Easter and is celebrated by Egyptians of all faiths.

general.q: Saint Catherine's Monastery, one of the oldest working Christian monasteries, lies at the foot of which mountain?
general.fact: Built in the 6th century, the monastery holds one of the oldest continually used libraries in the world.

general.q: What famous unfinished monument still lies in an ancient granite quarry at Aswan?
general.fact: Had it been completed, the Unfinished Obelisk would have stood about 42 m tall; it was abandoned after cracks appeared.

general.q: What did ancient Egyptians call their country, meaning "black land" after the dark Nile soil?
general.fact: Deshret, the "red land", was their word for the desert that surrounded the fertile black land of the valley.

general.q: Which lake does the Suez Canal pass through between Ismailia and Suez?
general.fact: During the canal's closure from 1967 to 1975, more than a dozen ships were trapped in the Great Bitter Lake and became known as the "Yellow Fleet".
